content: Stuttering, also known as stammering in some regions, is a speech disorder that disrupts a child's ability to speak fluently. It is a common condition, affecting approximately 11% of children by the age of four. Stuttering is characterized by repetitions of sounds, parts of words, or entire words, as well as sound prolongations or blockages in sound or airflow. These speech disruptions may be accompanied by non-verbal behaviors such as visible facial tension, eye blinking, or head nodding. Stuttering can also have negative impacts on a child's behavioral, social, and emotional well-being. The primary goal of this review was to evaluate the immediate and long-term effects of non-pharmacological interventions for stuttering in children aged six years and younger. The outcomes assessed included speech fluency, communication attitudes, quality of life, and any potential adverse effects. A secondary objective was to explore how intervention outcomes might vary based on participant characteristics, such as the child’s age, IQ, stuttering severity, sex, and the duration since stuttering onset. To gather relevant data, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including CENTRAL, MEDLINE, Embase, and PsycINFO, as well as trial registries, with no restrictions on language, publication year, or type of publication. Additional efforts included reviewing reference lists of included studies, contacting authors for unpublished data, and manually searching conference proceedings. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and quasi-RCTs that evaluated non-pharmacological interventions for stuttering in children aged six years or younger. Comparators included no intervention, wait-list controls, or usual management practices. Four eligible RCTs were identified, all of which compared the Lidcombe Program to a wait-list control group. A total of 151 children, aged between two and six years, participated in these studies. The Lidcombe Program involves parent-led treatment under the guidance of a speech and language therapist (SLT). Parents and children attend clinic visits, during which parents are trained to implement the therapy at home. In one study, clinic visits were conducted via telephone. The duration of the interventions varied, with two studies lasting nine months, one lasting 16 weeks, and another lasting 12 weeks. The frequency of clinic visits and home practice sessions also varied. Two studies were conducted in Australia, one in New Zealand, and one in Germany. Funding sources included the Rotary Club in Wiesbaden, Germany, and the National Health and Medical Research Council of Australia, while two studies either did not report funding or stated that no funding was received. All four studies reported outcomes related to stuttering frequency, measured as the percentage of syllables stuttered (% SS). One study also assessed speech efficiency, defined as the articulation rate. However, none of the studies reported on other pre-specified outcomes, such as stuttering severity, communication attitudes, emotional or psychosocial domains, or adverse effects. The Lidcombe Program was associated with a lower percentage of syllables stuttered (% SS) compared to the wait-list control group at post-test, as well as at 12 weeks, 16 weeks, and nine months post-randomization. The mean difference (MD) in % SS was −2.16 (95% confidence interval [CI]: −3.48 to −0.84; P = 0.001), based on very low-certainty evidence. However, it is important to note that none of the participants had completed the full Lidcombe Program, which typically takes one to two years to complete, at the time of data collection. The risk of bias in the included studies was high. Three of the four studies had a high risk of bias in at least one domain, while the fourth study had some concerns regarding bias. Moderate-certainty evidence from one study suggested that the Lidcombe Program may improve speech efficiency in young children. Only one study provided long-term follow-up data, but the results were incomplete for most children in the control group. A within-group comparison showed a significant reduction in stuttering frequency from randomization to extended follow-up. In conclusion, the Lidcombe Program may reduce stuttering frequency and improve speech efficiency in children aged six years and younger when compared to a wait-list control group. However, these findings should be interpreted with caution due to the very low to moderate certainty of the evidence and the high risk of bias in the included studies. Further research by independent investigators is needed to evaluate the immediate and long-term effects of other non-pharmacological interventions for stuttering in this population.
